title: Arion · lines 24–32
subtitle: Arion reaches Corinth, but Periander does not believe him until the sailors arrive and are confronted with the man they left for dead

units.en: He landed and went on to Corinth, still in his costume, and when he arrived he told the whole story.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Two participles cover a long journey across the Peloponnese in a few words, hurrying Arion back to Corinth.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: He walks to Corinth still in his performing robes. It is a striking picture, and the outfit will be the proof of his story.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: "Everything that had happened": Arion tells the full story, so Periander has every detail to test.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Periander's disbelief comes straight after his name, so his reaction is the first thing we learn about him here.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Periander keeps Arion under guard: he is a careful ruler who wants proof before he acts.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The strong negative shows how strictly Arion is held, which also keeps his return a secret.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.quote: Ἀρίονα μὲν … ἀνακῶς δὲ … τῶν πορθμέων
notes.body: Arion is dealt with on one side and the sailors on the other. The balance shows Periander handling both halves of the case.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.quote: ἤρετο εἴ τι λέγοιεν περὶ Ἀρίονος
notes.trans: he asked whether they had any news of Arion
notes.body: The question sounds innocent, but Periander and the reader know the truth and the sailors do not. We wait for them to walk into the trap.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The sailors claim that Arion is safe and doing well, which is true in a way they do not realise: he is safe, thanks to the dolphin.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.trans: that he was safe … and that they had left him
notes.body: τε … καί links two confident claims, so the lie sounds detailed and convincing just before it collapses.

notes.label: Tense
notes.body: The present participle catches the sailors in mid-sentence, and the aorist ἐπεφάνη marks Arion's sudden appearance. The timing is perfectly dramatic.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: This verb is often used of gods appearing to mortals, so Arion seems to come back from the dead.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: just as he was when he leapt
notes.body: ἐξεπήδησε repeats the verb the sailors used when they ordered him to jump (ἐκπηδᾶν, line 11), and ὥσπερ ἔχων recalls ὡς εἶχε (line 21). Their own words come back against them.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: A powerful verb, literally "knocked out of their senses": the sailors are stunned into silence.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The story ends on "to deny": the sailors' guilt is exposed and they are left with nothing to say.

questions: How well does Periander handle the situation? Would you have believed Arion?
Why is it important that Arion appears ὥσπερ ἔχων ἐξεπήδησε (line 31)?
The story ends without telling us how the sailors were punished. Why might Herodotus stop here?
Looking back over the whole story, how far is it about money, and how far about music?
